entry.title: From Entropy to Epiplexity: Rethinking Information for Computationally Bounded Intelligence

link.title: From Entropy to Epiplexity: Rethinking Information for Computationally Bounded Intelligence

entry.content:
Section 2: Randomness

1111111… isn’t random because LLN says that random strings should be 50% 0’s and 50% 1’s 1010101… isn’t random because it’s predictable

Martin-Lof randomness / Kolmogorov complexity: random if no short Turing machine can distinguish from true random

cryptographic randomness (pseudorandom number generator): no polynomial time alg can distinguish from true random

  • good enough in most settings because if you’re doing a polynomial time computation, then if using a PRG instead of a true RG made a difference, that would be a poly time alg to distinguish from true random

Section 3: Defining epiplexity

  • MDL = minimum description length = size of the program + entropy left using the program (think Occam’s razor, simplest program that explains it sufficiently)
  • Epiplexity is just the length of the program part. The rest of it is the “time-bounded entropy”
  • the time-bounded is from only allowing programs within a certain time complexity

Examples:

  • Uniform and Pseudo random number generators are low epiplexity high time-bounded entropy, since you can describe their minimum programs (the generators) pretty easily. Kolmogorov gives a somewhat higher complexity to PRGs; Gemini is telling me that this is mainly because epiplexity is defined on a random variable, while Kolmogorov complexity is defined on a fixed string, so you can hardcode the seed for the latter but not for the former. Hence, epiplexity concludes that there’s no poly-time learnable structure, while Kolmogorov complexity says that there is.

Section 4: Two methods of calculating Epiplexity on real datasets

Info theoretical setup: encoder has access to the test set $X$ and possibly teacher model checkpoints, decoder starts with just the base student model. They’re trying to minimize epiplexity (program length) + remaining entropy

  • epiplexity: we’re going to approximate programs as trained neural nets. Program length is roughly the number of bits / code that you need to transmit to a student, and the hard thing is how to measure the minimum number of bits that you need. There are two ways to do this:
    • prequential coding: you’re handing over the actual data over the channel. The decoder maintains their own synchronized copy of the model as the encoder is training it, and on step $i$, the encoder takes the next piece of data $Z$, uses the current model (that the decoder has) to calculate how many bits it is, and then sends that over the channel, and repeats for all the data.
      • this is too pessimistic, since it includes the remaining entropy of the data under the final trained model, so you adjust by subtracting the number of bits that you’d still have to send to encode the data if you had the trained model from the start. Note that this doesn’t tell you how to actually achieve the subtracted number of bits through a code, it’s non-constructive
      • this corresponds to area under the training loss curve (see below)
    • requential coding: instead of passing over real data, we can pass over synthetic data generated by the teacher checkpoints the encoder has access to.
      • This somehow takes less bits to encode, and furthermore is an explicit construction of the number of bits passed that we’re claiming.
      • This corresponds to the area between the loss curves
  • remaining entropy: after you have the trained model, you can just run a forward pass of the model on the test data $X$ to get the remaining entropy

And note that we’re trying to minimize this at an outer loop to find the MDL. They do this minimization just by trying a bunch of hyperparameters and taking the one with the lowest score.

  • prequential = area under the training loss curve
  • requential = area between the teacher and student loss curves

  • in practice, prequential and requential seem to agree. Prequential is cheaper since it just requires the one training run

Section 5. Epiplexity fixes 3 paradoxes of normal info theory

The common theme is just that restricting the computation of the observer explains the new information created in all three of these phenomena

5.1: post-processing doesn’t give new information

This is only true if you assume unlimited computation time. In that sense, run the deterministic AlphaZero RL doesn’t generate new information you didn’t have before. But it does if you don’t have the time to redo that computation

Notably, theoretically you only produce new information even with compute-constrained entropy if the inverse is not efficient. “some useful guidance for synthetic data: if we want to produce interesting information, we should make sure the functions we use do not have simple and efficiently computable inverses”

  • inverses means for instance deriving the original from the generated
  • do I believe this? I feel like this means most data augmentations are useless

  • three types of cellular automata synthetic data generation. Only rule 54 is high epiplexity

5.2 order should matter

Shannon entropy treats H(X, Y) and H(Y, X) the same, but time-bounded entropy doesn’t have to. Inferring the forward direction of a one-way function ought to be less entropy than the reverse direction

  • (a): forward direction of one-way function is easy to learn and approaches the Shannon entropy, the reverse direction doesn’t
  • (b, c): going from board position to chess moves is harder, but provides more structure / epiplexity to learn for larger compute regimes

5.3 The cap on what maximum likelihood modeling can learn is just to match the data generating process

5.3.1 “Induction” (not in the math sense, or in the induction heads sense)

Intuition for why this should be wrong: guessing the answer to a murder mystery (“induction”), which the model is trained for, is harder than being the author and knowing the murderer and just writing the murder mystery to be consistent with it

They mimic this by taking some bitstring $Z$, and applying some function $f$ to it, and also some masking $m(Z)$ to it, and only giving $(m(Z), f(Z))$ as the training pairs, so the model has to induct what the original $Z$ is from $m(Z)$.

Case 1: $f(Z)$ is a one-way function. Then the model just learns to brute force all $2^h$ missing bit combos for $Z$, and the irreducible loss is hence $h$. The epiplexity still grows as $h$ grows because transformers aren’t perfect Turing machines and hence can’t write for loops: the program size to iterate over $2^h$ combos grows as $h$ grows

Case 2: $f(Z)$ is a Markov chain with $h / 8$ of states not having known transitions. Then at $h=0$ it just learns to deterministically apply the rules, and at $h=8$ it learns to just use past empirics on the transitions, but at $0 < h < 8$ it has to combine both which leads to higher epiplexity

So the point being that epiplexity captures this kind of induction reasoning

5.3.2 “Emergent”

Conway’s game of life, if you have the compute (like a looped transformer) you can just brute force the computation, if not you need to think about gliders and what happens when they collide to predict the future and you learn more structure, more epiplexity.

  • at some level of compute, the brute force approach becomes possible and there’s less epiplexity because it just quickly learns that

Section 6: higher epiplexity predicts better OOD generalization

Intuition: epiplexity = learned general structure, irreducible loss is domain specific.

Of the two chess orderings from 5.2, the one with higher epiplexity generalizes better to predicting centipawn accuracy (more OOD than predict the next move puzzles)

  • They show that language pretraining data has a higher epiplexity content than image pretraining data

entry.title: Learning to Make MISTAKEs: Modeling Incorrect Student Thinking And Key Errors

link.title: Learning to Make MISTAKEs: Modeling Incorrect Student Thinking And Key Errors

entry.content:
The same motivation as me, be able to look at an example of a student mistake and figure out what their misconception was, and generate similar answers with those same misconceptions

They jointly train:

  1. a model that takes in the question and the wrong answer and produces the misconception, $M_m$
  2. a model that takes in the question and misconception and produces reasonable wrong answers, $M_s$

In a loop they

  1. Generate wrong answers to questions
  2. Use $M_m$ to infer the misconceptions
  3. Use $M_s$ to regenerate wrong answers from the misconception, and see if it matches the original wrong answer: this is their second key insight, that cycle consistency helps you filter out for good misconception data
  4. Fine-tune $M_m$ and $M_s$ on the resulting data

Experiments

Llama-3-8B-Instruct, kinda old models.

EEDI Mining Misconceptions in Mathematics dataset: K-12 math, MCQ questions with 4 choices. There’s misconception annotations for each of the wrong answer choices.

Their three metrics are

  1. Can $M_s$ correctly predict the wrong answer that the student chooses given the misconception (accuracy)
  2. How good are the misconceptions (some bs embedding similarity to the actual misconception)
  3. How good are the generated distractors after cycle consistency filters (by exact match to the chosen distractors)

Results are basically just that cycle consistency filter is important here, and they boost performance but still less than closed source models.

entry.title: Neural Cheat Sheets: Learning to Summarize with Reinforcement Learning

link.title: Neural Cheat Sheets: Learning to Summarize with Reinforcement Learning

entry.content:
RL’ing models to summarize in short natural text, where those summaries are then used to answer downstream MCQ Q&A

Main takeaway for my project: graph with accuracy and length being the two axes might be good.

They tried two different rewards on the summary, supervised and unsupervised

unsupervised: reconstruction cross entropy loss on the original document with vs without the summary, ish

  • You have to include a concave function on this, otherwise, the model learns to just copy the text directly, since that greatly decreases perplexity on the copied tokens and leaves everything else mostly unchanged

supervised: using the downstream QA directly

  • To get a denser reward signal, you can reward when the model has the higher gap over the second best answer

Experiments

Qwen3-4B, QuALITY (short stories), QASPER (NLP research papers), LongHealth (patient health records)

Results

  • I think we could make this graph, with size of the context vs accuracy compared to some other methods maybe (though we’re not directly apples-to-apples since we’re not doing summarization, though it somewhat can still hold)

  • this would just be misleading for us, as we’re not compaction

  • good generalization test, train on a bunch of summarization tasks and it boosts summarization performance for held-out domain, as much as if you trained on it directly. We can do similar generalization tests.

entry.title: IdeaLens: Detecting AI Ideas in Long-form Writing

link.title: IdeaLens: Detecting AI Ideas in Long-form Writing

entry.content:
They differentiate between AI-written vs AI ideas (where ideas is just operationalized as the outline from which the story is continued)

This is something I’ve been thinking about a lot, since I right now it’s somewhat of a negative signal to produce anything ai-sounding because you get lumped together with people who don’t put any thought in. But with something like IdeaLens instead, you could just differentiate out the people who don’t think about what they’re doing

  • they train on paraphrased outlines to predict whether it came from a human or AI, that way the model is forced to use the ideas (outline) instead of the style (the style is paraphrased by gemini for both AI and humans)
  • don’t know why they don’t paraphrase at test time

  • results: Pangram and models trained on just the prose can’t differentiate ideas
  • their contribution to the dataset is having AI generate the story outline and the human wrote the rest, upper right quadrant

analysis of AI vs human ideas

AI ideas are

  1. they’re overly general
  2. they overclaim

entry.title: Extending Tandem RLVR for training models to have legible outputs

link.title: Extending Tandem RLVR for training models to have legible outputs

entry.content:
Longer write-up  ·  Code  ·  🤗 Model checkpoints

This work was done as a mini group project for Boaz Barak’s AI safety class at Harvard (CS 2881r), together with Lance Bae and Marina Lin.

TL;DR: Tandem RLVR trains a strong “senior” model with GRPO while a frozen weaker “junior” model writes half of every rollout, with the goal of keeping the senior’s reasoning followable by the junior. Trained models are evaluated on two axes: solo performance (standard capability), where the model answers on its own, and handoff performance (a proxy for legibility), where each paragraph is randomly written by either the trained model or the frozen base model. We partially replicated the paper’s main experiment and ran three extensions:

  • Original setup (Qwen3-4B senior and junior): we matched the paper’s solo performance but not its handoff gains.
  • Larger capability gap (Qwen3.5-9B senior, Qwen3.5-2B junior): the handoff gains appeared.
  • Coding: Tandem RLVR hurt performance.
  • Elegant-vs-bashy math: Tandem rollouts favored bashier solutions during training, but the final model didn’t keep that preference when used on its own.

Introduction

Motivation

I’ve been thinking a lot recently about how to make LLM outputs more understandable to humans, and I came across the tandem training papers (Tandem Training and Tandem RLVR; my reading notes are here and here). As models get more capable, their reasoning can drift toward shorthand and approaches that are hard to follow. One proxy for legibility is whether a weaker model can pick up where the stronger model left off. Tandem training turns that proxy into a training signal.

What is Tandem RLVR?

During GRPO rollouts, a frozen junior model and the trainable senior co-write each response, with each word having a 50% chance of coming from either model. A verifier scores final-answer correctness, and GRPO only updates on senior-written tokens. Since the senior is only rewarded when the joint response is correct, it should learn to reason in a way the junior can continue.

Tandem RLVR's training loop. Figure 1 of Jiao et al.

The paper evaluates trained models in two modes:

  • Solo: the trained model answers on its own (normal usage).
  • Handoff: each paragraph is randomly written by either the trained model or the frozen base model. Handoffs are word-level during training and paragraph-level at evaluation, so evaluation is slightly held out.

The paper’s claim is that, compared to plain GRPO, Tandem RLVR gets similar solo performance while improving handoff performance.

Results

Exact reproduction on Qwen3-4B

We first tried to exactly reproduce Figure 2 of the paper. We used the authors’ codebase and hyperparameters: full-weight GRPO, 8 rollouts per problem, binary reward, 3,200 DeepScaleR training problems, no KL penalty, and a 3,000-token limit. We evaluated on AMC, AIME, Minerva, and OlympiadBench.

Handoff (top) and solo (bottom) pass@k. Tandem matches GRPO solo, but does not improve handoff.

Solo performance matched the paper: both GRPO and Tandem clearly beat the base model. The handoff improvement did not reproduce. For example, macro-average handoff pass@8 was 61.8% for GRPO and 60.5% for Tandem.

Extension 1: Larger senior-junior gap

We guessed that the effect might be clearer if the junior were meaningfully weaker than the senior, so we switched to a Qwen3.5-9B senior with a frozen Qwen3.5-2B junior (non-thinking mode, matching the original Instruct setup).

With a 9B senior and 2B junior, Tandem improves average handoff performance while matching solo.

This looks much more like the original paper: the Tandem senior does better on handoff and matches GRPO solo. Minerva was inconsistent. Its results were also unusual in the original paper, and we found and fixed some Minerva-specific grading bugs in the codebase, but that didn’t fully resolve it.

Extension 2: Coding

All the original experiments were in math, so we tried APPS (LeetCode-style Python problems) with otherwise identical hyperparameters. Our prior was that coding would be harder for Tandem: one bad junior token in a long program could break the whole solution, whereas math has a short critical final answer.

On APPS, Tandem RLVR is worse than GRPO on both handoff and solo, and slightly worse than the base model solo.

Tandem did do worse, even falling below the base model solo, but our explanation was wrong. We took correct solo solutions, found a position where the senior’s and junior’s top tokens differ, forced the junior’s token, and let the senior continue. Success only dropped by about 2 points:

SeniorSolutionsControl successJunior token forced
GRPO35096.4%94.8%
Tandem27697.6%95.2%

So single junior tokens don’t derail code much, and we don’t yet have a good explanation for why Tandem underperforms here.

Extension 3: Elegant vs. bashy solutions

Everything above uses handoff performance as a stand-in for legibility. We wanted a more direct measure. We first tried to get plain GRPO to produce jargon (including with a length penalty), hoping Tandem would prevent it, but GRPO never produced jargon in the first place.

Instead, we built a dataset of 374 AIME-level problems from HARP, each with multiple solution paths. Some are short and elegant (e.g., a symmetry or complementary-counting argument), others bashy but easier to follow (e.g., casework over every possibility). A GPT-6.1 Sol judge labeled each reference path and grades the model’s new solutions. To push toward elegance, elegant correct solutions got 50% extra reward. Our hypothesis was that Tandem training should push the senior toward bashy solutions, since those are easier for the junior to continue.

As a sanity check, the untrained 9B model does prefer elegant solutions more than the 2B model (52.6% vs. 36.3% of correct solutions, on the 55 problems both solve).

(a) The untrained 9B prefers elegant solutions more than the 2B. (b) During training, tandem rollouts are consistently less elegant than GRPO rollouts. (c) But the final Tandem senior is as elegant as the GRPO senior in both solo and handoff modes.

During training, tandem rollouts were consistently less elegant than GRPO rollouts, as predicted. But this did not carry over to the trained senior: evaluated on its own, it picks elegant solutions as often as the GRPO model.

Takeaways

  • Tandem RLVR does not work robustly. The paper’s results didn’t hold up in our exact reproduction or on coding, although they did with a larger senior-junior gap.
  • Legible tandem rollouts don’t produce a legible senior. In the elegance experiment, Tandem RLVR rollouts favored bashier, more legible solutions throughout training, but the trained senior didn’t keep that preference when run on its own. This undercuts the core intuition behind Tandem RLVR: that rewarding the senior for joint rollouts the junior can follow will make the senior’s own outputs more legible.
  • Handoff performance is a weak proxy for legibility. Building tasks where plain RL actually makes outputs less legible was harder than we expected. That seems like an important open problem for evaluating methods like this.

For full details, including example problems and the judge prompt, see the longer write-up.
entry.summary: Partially replicating Tandem RLVR and testing whether it generalizes to bigger capability gaps, coding, and elegant-vs-bashy math

entry.title: Shared Geometry as a Rosetta Stone Cross-Modal Alignment Without Paired Data

link.title: Shared Geometry as a Rosetta Stone Cross-Modal Alignment Without Paired Data

entry.content:
Updated with notes from Dominik’s talk on 10/14

website demo is really convincing https://dominik-schnaus.github.io/unpaired-rosetta/

align text embeddings from Qwen3-8B and image embeddings from DINOv2 without any labeled image-caption pairs!

Math / Figure 2

This is the main objective they’re trying to optimize:

We want two things:

  1. $W$, a $d_X \times d_Y$ mapping from the text embedding space to the vision embedding space
  2. $T$, where $T_{ij}$ is $1$ if text data point $i$ maps to image data point $j$ and $0$ otherwise.

Right: initialization of candidates for $W$ and $M$:

  1. We first want a reasonable initialization for $W$
    1. (line 6) We do k-means clustering on both text space and image space separately.
    2. (line 7) Then, we pair clusters in text and vision space to each other by checking through all permutations $P$ (in practice, they do this using some quadratic programming) of the clusters on one side and finding the permutation with highest CKA similarity between the clusters (CKA similarity depends on the ordering of the clusters), which ensures that the similarity between cluster $\ell$ and cluster $r$ in text-space should be close to the similarity between cluster $\ell$ and cluster $r$ in corresponding clusters in image space.
    3. (line 8) Using this pairing $P$, we construct the first candidate for $W$, which they call $M$.
      1. if you just do one clustering it’s possible that the clusters don’t match up exactly (one cluster might not have an equivalent in the other space), hence why they needed to average over many clusterings.
      2. the batching is just for computational efficiency of the matching, can only match b to b points at a time
  2. Freezing this $W$, they construct the first candidate for $T$. By the above, $XMY^T$ is the similarity scores $s_{ij}$ between all points $i$ and $j$. Hungarian matching then solves for the optimal matching $T$ trying to minimize the sum of the similarity scores $s_{ij}$ between matched points.

Left: Wasserstein Procrustes to iteratively improve $W$ and $M$

  1. Line 5/9: If you freeze $T$, you can solve for the closed form $W$ which optimizes the equation (1) objective using some SVD

  1. Line 8: now freeze $W$ and then solve for the best $T$, the same as we did in Right panel step

  2. Repeatedly refine $W$ and $T$. For the refinement part, you don’t even need to take an EWMA of the W, it stabilizes on its own as you keep taking batches and rewriting the entire $W$ using just the current batch.

Experiments

Method details

used last hidden state for all embeddings (didn’t ablate this), tried 3 different token poolings (sophie’s, mean pooled over tokens, qwen3-emb EOS token)

k=30 chosen just because that’s what their NP opt solver can do, would want more clusters if possible

They use FOS-CTTM as their main metric: if you take a text embedding $x$ and and map it using $W$ to an image embedding $y$, and you have the ground truth pairings between e.g. images $x$ and their captions $y$, then out of all the images, what fraction of them are closer to $Wx$ than $y$ is? Ideally, this number is $0$

  • (a) in the first column, they train on unpaired captions and images from different datasets, and then just validate the learned $W$ using matched image-caption pairs on MS COCO.
  • (c) if the actual image-caption pairs are more CKA aligned, the method works better
  • dinov2 much better than dinov3 — maybe the embedding extraction should be different
  • qwen3 generative embeddings worse with long captions — embedding model already has enough to work with, don’t need to generate

  • works on bio model spaces to bio model spaces

entry.title: Can SAEs Capture Neural Geometry?
entry.content:
Recall that lots of concepts are represented in activation space as manifolds (found via just varying the inputs, getting the activations, and then PCA’ing them down and seeing that they vary continuously)

SAEs are trying to capture this in a linear subspace. This explains a lot of the failures behind SAEs:

Theoretically, SAEs could try to capture the manifold in one of these three ways

  • In practice, they just do dilution, which means that messily, each point on the manifold corresponds to a lot of feature directions, and each feature direction covers a sub-region of the manifold

You can try to reverse engineer the manifold from groups of correlated SAE features

  • they should be correlated (in an Ising model sense) because, for instance, if you consider a feature for each day of the week, only one of these features should be on at each time

But they believe that you can decompose activation space into a superposition of low-dimensional manifolds

  • reverse engineering from SAEs is probably not the right way to go about finding these manifolds

entry.title: Finetuning with Sampling: SFT Learns Better Than You Think

link.title: Finetuning with Sampling: SFT Learns Better Than You Think

entry.content:
Updated with Aayush Karan’s invited talk / Q&A on 10/13

SFT causes catastrophic forgetting and generalization issues due to being off-policy. But RL struggles with capabilities that the base model didn’t have to begin with (e.g. 0/8 rollouts solve it)

Prior work motivation

https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.14901 in a previous work, he shows that if you sample entire sequences (using the same metropolis hastings technique as this paper will use) to try to sample sequences from a power-law sharpened distribution instead of from the original output distribution, you basically get GRPO-level performance training-free.

This motivates using sampling as an algorithmic primitive

  • This is different from low temperature/greedy sampling because it’s sharpening the distribution on sequences, not on tokens

Theoretical Motivation

Their method’s idea is to try to transform SFT data to be more on-distribution:

Suppose that $x \in \mathcal{C}$ is the set of all rollouts where the answer is correct, and $p(x)$ is the base model’s distribution over rollouts. The closest distribution (in KL) $q$ to $p$ which has support only on $C$ is \(p_{\mathcal{C}}(x) \propto p(x) \cdot \mathbf{1}\{ x \in \mathcal{C} \}\)We’d like to get our SFT data to look like it was drawn from $p_{\mathcal{C}}(x)$.

Of course, you can get this distribution by just sampling from $p$ and rejecting until you get $x \in \mathcal{C}$, but what if it’s very low probability? It’s only making use of the privileged correct answer information as a verifier, when we would like to use it to generate the data. To do this, we can use Metropolis Hastings

For metropolis hastings, you need your target stationary distribution up to normalization constant, and a proposal distribution $\kappa(x \mid x’)$ for the transition probability between states.

  • this is the acceptance probability that you multiply by when moving from $x’$ to $x$
    • recall Metropolis-hastings makes it so that the probability flow from $x \to x’$ is and $x’ \to x$ are both the same, and equal to the min under the proposal distribution
  • you can get rid of the \(\mathbf{1}\{ x \in \mathcal{C} \}\) if you make sure that your transitions are only on $\mathcal{C}$.

Empirics and Results

In practice, the method looks like

  1. Take off a suffix of the current generation, use the base model prompted with the correct answer as the proposer
  • this is an approximation to actual conditioning on $x \in \mathcal{C}$
  1. Accept the new sample if it has higher likelihood under the base model than the current completion
  • This is an approximation to the metropolis-hastings acceptance condition. They do this just for speed reasons: $\kappa(x \mid x’)$ and $\kappa(x’ \mid x)$ require two LLM forward passes in the Metropolis-Hastings, and they’d rather just spend one

For data where the answer is not verifiable, they use LLM judge consistency with the original answer from the offline SFT ground truth.

Compare to on-policy self-distillation: https://siyan-zhao.github.io/blog/2026/opsd/: they also use the model prompted with the correct answer as a teacher model, but instead of changing the training data (which is still generated by the model being trained), they just edit the loss to be a distillation KL loss

Qwen2.5-7B, Olmo-3-7B, Chemistry, MMLU, AMC

  • Seems like it does result in more on-policy SFT data
  • Note that likelihood is just a proxy for on-policyness, the exact measure is the KL distance between the model policies, which they kept track of and made sure was also decreasing as they sampled

  • Less forgetting, higher accuracy.
  • they have Table 1 showing that it beats GRPO too

  • Through this SFT, it genuinely learns new capabilities that it got 0% success rate on before
  • Doesn’t suffer from mode collapse like RL causes

Miscellaneous Q&A answers

Computational inefficiency: it’s epoch-agnostic, so takes about as long as a 32-epoch RL run if you need that many epochs. Not very efficient.

Resampling as weights change: Similar to RL, you probably want to regenerate the data to be on policy again after doing some SFT weight changes. However, if the SFT dataset is small enough, like the ones used here, you don’t need to do this, just for computational efficiency

entry.title: Tandem Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards

link.title: Tandem Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards

entry.content:
follow-up to tandem training

Tandem training using GRPO and initializing the senior and junior model to both be Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507

  • Unlike the tandem training paper, they finally only update on the senior-generated tokens from the rollout

Data: trained on DeepScaleR math, evaluated on AMC, AIME, Minerva, Olympiad (all math)

Results

  • pass@k with k as the x-axis
  • Bottom row: When evaluated solo, the tandem trained model has approximately the same performance as the GRPO’d model
  • Top row: When you hand off to the other model after every sentence (note that they’re trained to hand off every word, so this is a little bit generalization), tandem is a little better than GRPO
    • TRLVR beats KL-regularization as a baseline

  • A bunch of sketchy metrics showing that the distribution of tokens outputted by the tandem trained model is closer to the base model than GRPO.
    • Seems that tandem gives more failure/transitioning words, and GRPO gives more formatting

  • The base model is less surprised about the words generated by the tandem model than the GRPO model

Implementation details

They had to fork vLLM because if you try to do the obvious thing of just using Hugging Face and manually managing the KV cache, it’s apparently too slow.

The best you can do is half the throughput, since you do need to always be generating both forward passes, since you need to maintain both KV caches

word boundaries are determined by tokens which began with a space, or by 32 tokens in a row, whichever one happens first

  • training dynamics should look somewhat reasonable

Misc remarks

Their introduction has a few really nice points about the effect of RLVR on reasoning:

  • https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.22446 alibaba qwen shows that RLVR only really drastically changes the token distributions for a sparse set of tokens
  • https://arcprize.org/blog/astra Astra created its own compact algebraic notation for solving ARC Agi 3
  • https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.09867 There are apparently some actual examples of obfuscated reasoning in the stolen chain of thoughts here

entry.title: Tandem Training for Language Models
entry.content:
Do RL, except on the rollouts, on every word randomly (50%) let a frozen dumber model sample the next word instead of the smarter model actually being trained

  • The idea is that this forces the smarter model to reason in a more legible, less jargony manner
  • Having a more understandable reasoning output seems like a good thing. Not sure how this works with chain of thought models though.

Experiments

GSM8K, Llama-2-7B

“smarter” senior model = fine-tuned on GSM8k

also create some dumber junior model variants by prompting them with some few-shot examples to speak in a different language

  • GSM8k’s solutions involve repeating all arithmetic in « », which they call jargon (only the SFT’d model does it)
  • they also call speaking in a language that the junior model doesn’t speak in “jargon”

For some reason they use REINFORCE (1 epoch) and discard negative rollouts instead of GRPO or something. Not sure why.

Results

Accuracy does fall, but it remains a little higher than the dumber model.

The rate of jargon goes to zero, though, pretty quickly
